Ti–O thermodynamics · Vlachos Group

Gas–solid equilibrium

Calculates the equilibrium phase assemblage and gas composition for a specified Ti–O–gas inventory.

Rutile defect thermodynamics · Vlachos Group

Defect-state distribution

Calculates the equilibrium distribution of a measured oxygen-vacancy inventory across rutile sites.

Oxygen-carrier redox · Vlachos Group

Steady-state redox

Solves the crossing of the two half-reaction rates, and says whether a carrier can be run there.

Model scope and assumptions
Scope. C–H–O–N / Ti–O Gibbs equilibrium. Gas registry in this version: CO2, H2, CO, H2O, N2, O2. Hydrocarbon species (CH4), graphite, nitrides, and the rutile TiO2−x solution phase are not included in this version. The calculation is a closed, finite-inventory equilibrium between one gas charge and one solid charge, not a flow-reactor steady state. Every reported value is gibbs_min.
Loaded as this phase; the equilibrium assemblage is an output.

Condensed phases

Gas: initial and equilibrium

How far from a different answer

The same question the KKT tab answers in numbers, asked twice: across the phases that were excluded at this condition, and across temperature at this charge. Both bars and curve carry the reduced cost per formula unit — the quantity the KKT test is stated on, so it is positive at every reported solution. The per‑mol‑O column stays on the KKT tab, next to the oxygen deficiency it is divided by, which changes sign whenever a candidate is less deficient than the host.

121 solves at this charge, about half a second.

Active set and KKT reduced costs

Phase stability is decided by the sign of the reduced cost. rj > 0: the phase is absent. |rj| within tolerance: phase boundary. Negative values do not occur at a reported solution.

Method

The solver computes the minimum of the total Gibbs energy

G = Σgas ni [μ°i(T) + RT ln(yiP/P°)] + Σsolid mj μ°j(T)

subject to the elemental balance A·n = b and n ≥ 0. Gases form an ideal mixture; each condensed phase is a pure line compound at unit activity. The inputs defining b are the initial gas composition, the gas charge ng,0 = PV/RTcharge, and the initial solid phase and mass. The equilibrium phase split is an output.

Active set. Condensed phases are enumerated as candidates: every single phase and every phase pair (the phase rule allows two line compounds in an M–O system at fixed T and P; N2 adds no solid component). For each candidate the equilibrium conditions are

gas:  μi = Σe aieλe    active solids:  μ°j = tjλTi + ojλO

solved by Newton iteration in the element potentials λ with the gas in logarithmic coordinates. Condensed amounts follow linearly from the Ti and O balances through the combination O − ρhost·Ti, which removes the host oxygen symbolically; coexisting phases are resolved down to ~10−41 mol. A phase outside the candidate is not a variable and is exactly zero in the result.

Stability criterion. Each inactive phase carries a reduced cost rj = μ°j − tjλTi − ojλO, reported per formula unit and per mole of oxygen (defj = 2tj − oj; defj = 1 for each TiO2→Magnéli step). The problem is convex, so a feasible candidate with all rj ≥ 0 is the global minimum. Candidates are not ranked by total Gibbs energy, whose differences can fall below double-precision resolution. Reduced costs at zero within tolerance are reported as phase coexistence.

Oxygen-free feeds. Under pure H2 or N2 the single-phase candidate leaves the gas with zero oxygen inventory, and the derivative of G toward forming a trace of O-bearing gas together with a reduced phase diverges. The solver therefore reports the two-phase buffer with a finite trace amount; under sealed N2 this trace is the equilibrium result. An O2 impurity at the ppm level is sufficient to suppress reduction, with a positive margin.

The oxygen-potential margin used by earlier versions of this site equals the reduced cost per mole of oxygen (the dual of the same minimisation); it is reported on the Active set & KKT tab. Independent verification is provided by an 80-digit reference implementation and by the NIST–Waldner data comparison (Validation tab).

Earlier pages from this repository, kept for provenance. They run the

TiOx oxygen-potential dashboard: critical
      oxygen potentials swept across temperature with the phase boundaries drawn. Its margin

First-generation Gibbs solver: the

Why these pages are retired. The earlier engine represented
      absent phases at a logarithmic floor (~10−17–10−26
      percent) rather than at zero, which cannot be distinguished by magnitude from a genuine
      trace amount (under sealed N2, ~10−36 percent is the
      equilibrium result). The engine on this page holds absent phases at exactly zero,
      reports a KKT reduced cost instead, and is pinned to an 80-digit reference by the
      repository test suite. Trace values on the legacy pages are solver residue, not phases;
      their CH4-feed results assume no carbon deposition and are conditional.

    


  













Model scope and assumptions


  Scope. Canonical lattice statistical mechanics for a measured oxygen-vacancy
  inventory in rutile TiO2: the total VO is fixed from experiment
  and its conditional-equilibrium partition over (110) bridging-O, first-subsurface and
  bulk sites is computed at equal vacancy chemical potential — the thermodynamic
  tendency for redistribution of a prescribed inventory, not reduction kinetics.
  Site energies are polaron-relaxed literature DFT values; Ti3+ polarons are
  not explicit variables in this version. The reported 17–20% onset of the
  (1×2) reconstruction is treated as a competing surface phase, not a cap:
  at the onset the (1×1) vacancy lattice gas coexists with the added-row
  Ti2O3 line phase (lever rule at pinned μV,
  areal O deficiency 0.5 bridging-ML), and beyond the bulk point-defect solubility
  μV pins at the estimated rutile/CS coexistence with the excess reported
  as extended defects. Nothing is clipped and no remainder is silently reassigned;
  the idealisations of each phase branch are declared in data/rutile_dft.json.






Oxygen environment


The status line beside the controls is the equilibrium
workspace’s charge — gas, pressure, volume and solid —
evaluated by the gas–solid Gibbs engine at the defect temperature. It
bounds this workspace rather than feeding it: the defect model describes
point defects in rutile, and the equilibrium verdict says whether rutile is
the phase to be in. Open the equilibrium workspace to change the charge.



Reoxidation kinetics


Placeholder kinetics: first-order refill per class,
kc = Ac pm e−Ea/kT,
Pc = 1 − e−kt. The prefactors are effective
because deeper classes are transport-limited. None of these numbers is a
literature value; every derived recoverable fraction is
illustrative until fitted to the CO2 recovery measurements. The transport layer is
the group’s coarse-grained KMC (Katsoulakis & Vlachos, J. Chem.
Phys. 119, 9412 (2003)): radial coarse cells over the particle,
detailed-balance exchange rates against the same site-class Hamiltonian, and
the irreversible surface refill as the only gas channel. Em
defaults to the neutral-vacancy bulk barrier (Iddir et al.).



Sampling


A run samples the surface isotherm
θs(μV) for the current temperature and
energetics in a Web Worker (canonical swap Metropolis, Widom insertion).
Inventory and particle size re-solve instantly without a new run. The second
input mode — thermodynamic μO, grand-canonical —
arrives with absolute DFT formation free energies; this version is canonical,
at a measured VO.



Dataset


Layer energetics: Li, Guo & Robertson, J. Phys. Chem. C
119 (2015). Surface ordering: Birschitzky et al., npj Comput. Mater. 10
(2024). Diffusion barriers: Iddir et al., J. Phys. Chem. C (2010); Wang et
al., Phys. Rev. B 82 (2010). Cross-row terms and the 10 Å cutoff are
fixed in data/rutile_dft.json.



Formulation and references


      
We calculate the conditional-equilibrium partitioning of the measured vacancy
      inventory to determine the thermodynamic tendency for vacancy redistribution
      among surface, subsurface and bulk environments. Three site classes hold the
      fixed total: rutile (110) bridging O, the first subsurface O layer (the in-plane
      and sub-bridging O of the outer trilayer — removal of non-bridging oxygen
      is this class), and bulk. The partition equalises the vacancy chemical potential
      using the analytic site-exclusion isotherms on the formation energies alone.
      Surface lateral ordering is a separate calculation: effective pair interactions,
      constrained to reproduce the vacancy-correlation statistics reported by
      Birschitzky et al., are sampled by canonical Metropolis Monte Carlo with Widom
      insertion, and inform the arrangement exhibits only — they never enter the
      layer partition.

      
Shell thickness is a declared model choice, not a fitted quantity. The
      (1×1) cell carries one bridging O, while every d110 = 0.325 nm
      oxygen slab below the bridging plane carries four O per cell, so one subsurface
      layer is four bridging rows of capacity (54.2 against 13.6 μmol-O/g at
      0.9 μm) and the class is never a single atomic row. The default of one layer
      follows the DFT set, which resolves one first-subsurface energy and takes deeper
      layers as bulk. Because that energy lies far below the bulk value, the shell/bulk
      split moves with the choice: at 600 °C and 95 μmol-O/g the subsurface class
      holds 51.8 / 82.6 / 86.3 / 87.1 μmol-O/g for one to four layers, the bulk takes
      36.5 / 5.6 / 2.0 / 1.2, and μV falls from 0.819 to 0.560 eV. Real
      formation energies relax smoothly towards the bulk value over the first few
      layers, so the physical answer lies between the one- and two-layer columns. What
      moves is the size of the bulk remainder, not the conclusion that the near-surface
      shell carries most of the inventory (62% of it at one layer, 94% at two). The
      ladder is certified against the 50-digit oracle and the control in the input
      panel reproduces it.

      
Two phase branches close the construction. The (1×2) reconstruction
      enters as a first-order surface transition at the reported onset: the (1×1)
      lattice gas coexists with the added-row Ti2O3 line phase
      (Onishi–Iwasawa stoichiometry, one O vacancy per two bridging sites,
      θeff = 0.5; confirmed stable under reduction by Reticcioli et
      al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031053 (2017)), with the lever rule at pinned
      μV. The high-coverage branch of the ideal (1×1) gas is
      excluded from the phase set on physical grounds (repulsive ordering energies;
      the observed strongly reduced surface is reconstructed, not bridging-stripped).
      Beyond the bulk point-defect solubility (xsol ≈ 0.008 in
      TiO2−x, an estimate), μV pins at the rutile/CS
      coexistence and the excess precipitates as extended defects. The particle-scale
      balance uses the real geometric site counts: at 0.9 μm the bridging-O layer
      holds at most 13.6 μmol-O/g (0.054% of all O sites), so a 95 μmol-O/g
      inventory drives the surface through the reconstruction (complete by
      ∼6.8 μmol-O/g) and loads the subsurface shell to ∼95% occupancy,
      just below the estimated CS ceiling (∼160 μmol-O/g at 600 °C).
      The certified boundary ladder is printed above the results; the measured BET
      area (1.60 m²/g) and the diameter model agree on it to ∼2%.

      
Site energies are polaron-relaxed DFT values: the oxygen vacancy itself is most
      stable in the surface layer, while the Ti3+ small polarons it donates
      prefer subsurface Ti (Reticcioli et al., Phys. Rev. B 98, 045306 (2018)). The
      single subsurface energy is applied to all four O sites of the first layer
      (a data-granularity limit; per-site project DFT will split the class in the
      dataset). Explicit polaron variables and the grand-canonical coupling to the
      gas-phase oxygen potential are later stages of this workspace. The kinetic
      transport layer implements the group's coarse-grained kinetic Monte Carlo
      framework (Katsoulakis & Vlachos, J. Chem. Phys. 119, 9412 (2003), DOI
      10.1063/1.1616513; Katsoulakis, Majda & Vlachos, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA
      100, 782 (2003)): detailed-balance exchange rates on radial coarse cells,
      reducing in the dilute limit to spherical diffusion, with the CO2
      surface refill as the one irreversible channel.

      
Dataset. Layer energies: Li, Guo & Robertson, J. Phys. Chem. C 119
      (2015), DOI 10.1021/acs.jpcc.5b02430: sX 0 / +0.59 / +1.31 eV, GGA
      0 / +0.39 / +1.08 eV (surface / first subsurface / bulk); the ordering survives the
      change of functional. Surface ordering constraints: Birschitzky et al., npj Comput.
      Mater. 10 (2024), DOI 10.1038/s41524-024-01289-4: in-row spacings of 1–2
      bridging sites nearly absent, modal spacing 4–5 sites, experimental average
      reconstruction onset ∼17%, DFT transition ∼20%, locally rich regions up
      to ∼20%, and interaction range ∼10 Å. These percentages define a
      reconstruction interval and do not define a maximum vacancy capacity.
      The pair energies here are calibrated to those constraints. Project DFT
      configuration energies will replace them directly when those values
      arrive. Every model parameter lives in data/rutile_dft.json. Dielectric
      correlation: measured in this work. The power-law fit and its statistics are
      shown on the accessibility panel. Diffusion barriers stored for kinetics:
      Iddir et al., J. Phys. Chem. C (2010); Wang et al., Phys. Rev. B 82, 165309
      (2010).

      
The browser engine is a line-for-line port of
      solidgas/statmech.py, pinned move-for-move to the Python reference
      (same-seed swap trajectories compared as integers) and to a 50-digit analytic
      oracle plus exact finite-lattice ensembles by the repository test suite
      (tests/test_statmech.py, tests/test_statmech_port.py).

Vacancy distribution

        
Conditional-equilibrium partition of the measured
        inventory at the common vacancy chemical potential, over the real
        geometric site counts of the particle. The (1×2) reconstruction
        and the CS ceiling enter as phases.

        
        

        

        

      


      

        
The same inventory, resolved by depth

        
The partition above splits the particle into a
        bridging row, one subsurface slab and everything else. This card
        answers the same question with a depth coordinate instead: the
        vacancy formation energy relaxes towards the bulk value over a
        decay length derived from the DFT triple rather than an
        assumed profile shape, and the interior is summed as the stack of
        d110 oxygen layers it physically is. It also makes two
        checks the class model has no way to state — whether the
        equilibrium is reachable inside the exposure, and whether local
        electroneutrality is allowed. Engine:
        solidgas/particle/, mirrored in
        web/particle.js.

        

        

          
          
        

        
State

        

        
Is the equilibrium reachable?

        
A Crank sphere-diffusion clock against the
        exposure. Claiming transport is fast is only worth something with
        the distance to it not being fast, so the barrier that would
        close the gap is reported next to the literature one.

        

        
Is local electroneutrality allowed?

        
The profile assumes each vacancy drags its two
        polarons with it pointwise. That holds when screening is much
        shorter than segregation. Both lengths are computed here rather
        than inherited from the ceria case this construction comes
        from, which ran an order of magnitude more concentrated.

        

      


      

        
Particle cross-section

        
Spherical particle cross-section. The outer shell is
        magnified at right on an isotropic scale, so
        one drawn dot is one vacancy on one oxygen site: the bridging
        plane carries one O per
        (1×1) column and each 0.325 nm layer below it carries four. The
        bridging row shows the sampled Monte Carlo arrangement, the subsurface
        sites use the calculated class occupancy, and the core fill tracks the
        bulk occupancy as a tint rather than placed vacancies, because the
        partition carries no depth structure inside the bulk class. The
        lower panel shows the same three values against radial depth.

        
        
        

      

    


    

      

        
CO2-accessible inventory

        
First-order refill of each site class during one
        CO2 exposure, applied to the distribution. The figure walks
        the phase ladder along a total-inventory axis: the surface crosses the
        (1×2) coexistence riser and holds at the line-phase deficiency,
        the subsurface shell fills, and beyond the estimated CS ceiling the
        excess precipitates as extended defects.

        

        
        

        

      

    


    

      

        
Reoxidation kinetics — CGMC

        
Coarse-grained kinetic Monte Carlo of the whole particle
        during one CO2 exposure: radial coarse cells, Arrhenius
        exchange rates in detailed balance with the (1×1) site-class
        Hamiltonian, and the irreversible surface refill as the only gas
        channel. With the neutral-vacancy barrier, transport is not
        rate-limiting at 600 °C — a measured partial recovery
        therefore reads back as an effective migration barrier.

        

        
        
        

      

    

  















Model scope and assumptions


  Scope. Steady-state Mars–van Krevelen redox of an oxygen carrier under
  simultaneous exposure to a reductant and an oxidant. The reductant takes lattice oxygen
  and leaves a vacancy; the oxidant fills a vacancy and puts lattice oxygen back. Nothing
  adsorbs and there are no surface intermediates: the two steps are written straight onto
  the lattice-oxygen site balance. The solid is one number, the vacancy fraction θ
  on the reacting oxygen sites, and the steady state is where the two half-reaction rates
  cross. Mass action, unit site orders, one crossing — nothing here is
  methodologically new, and that is the point: the question the model is asked is which
  carriers can be run at their own optimum, not how to compute a rate.

  
What θ counts. Vacancies on the two-coordinate bridging oxygen rows
  of rutile (110), as a fraction of those sites. That is the site the descriptor is
  referenced to — Evac = 4.39 eV for (110) bridging O, sX hybrid, Li, Guo
  & Robertson 2015 — and it is where the face ceiling comes from:
  θmax = 0.5 is the (1×2) added-row reconstruction, which is a
  bridging-row phase. Three-coordinate in-plane oxygen is not counted. It is held
  more strongly, so its removal energy is not the descriptor's, and putting both into one
  θ would average two different sites into a number that describes neither. The
  price of not doing that is that the reacting inventory here is the bridging rows alone:
  a mechanism that consumes in-plane oxygen is outside this model, and so is any face
  other than (110).


  
θ is not a defect population. The particle-average θ is
  stoichiometric bookkeeping, x/2 in MO(2−x), and carries no claim about which
  defect holds the reduction. In rutile at low x the majority point defect is the titanium
  interstitial rather than the oxygen vacancy, and past the solubility the solid stops
  making point defects at all and relieves reduction by crystallographic shear. The face
  θ is a coverage on a named site; the particle θ is a composition. They are
  different kinds of quantity, which is why the model keeps them apart.


  
The axis. At unit site orders the crossing is
  θ(face) = K / (1 + K) with K = k(reduction) / k(oxidation), exactly, with no
  temperature, no pressure and no prefactor left in it. Only the ratio of the two
  rate constants is a material property of the carrier; the absolute values set how fast
  it gets there, not where it lands. Every richer parameterisation — fitted rate
  constants, a computed vacancy formation energy fed through Brønsted–Evans–Polanyi
  slopes — is a way of predicting K, and each adds an assumption the closed form
  does not need. Those live in solidgas/redox.py and are deliberately not
  on this page.


  
The two limits. A crossing is not the same thing as an operating point. The
  solid must stay one phase, θ(particle) ≤ θsol, or the
  vacancies order into a second structure (in rutile, crystallographic shear planes) and
  mass action in θ has left its domain. And the reacting face must stay below the
  occupancy its own surface phase pins it at, θ(face) ≤ θmax;
  past that the oxidation rate stops rising with the inventory, the imbalance keeps its
  sign, and there is no steady state to settle into.


  
The uniform assumption, and its price. The two limits are connected by
  E = θ(face) / θ(particle), the surface enrichment. A uniform particle sets
  E = 1 without saying so; a layer-resolved partition supplies it. Holding E fixed while
  the carrier turns over is a statement about timescales, not only about geometry:
  the face and the interior are taken to be in equilibrium partition at every instant, so
  oxygen exchange between shell and bulk is fast compared with both half-reactions. If it
  is not — if the interior cannot resupply the face on the turnover timescale
  — this is the wrong model, and the problem becomes transport into the particle
  rather than a boundary condition on it. The partition itself is the defect workspace's
  equilibrium answer, so the assumption is inherited from there and not made twice. For 0.9 µm rutile
  at 600 °C the defect workspace gives E ≈ 1844, against a geometric ceiling of
  1847 — nearly every vacancy is in the shell. That moves the largest usable K from
  0.0040 to 1, a factor of 249. The turnover at a given K is unchanged by the
  correction, because any strictly increasing average→face mapping only
  reparameterises the same crossing; what changes is the inventory the particle must
  hold to keep the face there, and therefore whether the solid survives it.


  
What is assumed. Unit gas and site orders in both half-reactions; one
  reacting face, (110), and one oxygen site on it, the bridging row; shell–bulk
  exchange fast enough that the enrichment is an equilibrium partition; no gradient within
  the particle beyond that single factor; no transport limitation; the solubility as an
  estimate carried as a sensitivity parameter. The reductant and the oxidant are left
  unnamed on purpose: the rate parameters in the dataset are identical placeholders for
  both halves, so naming a gas pair would assert chemistry the numbers do not carry. Any
  pair that is first order in gas and in site gives the same K axis. Parameters and their provenance are in data/redox.json, each
  labelled literature, estimate or assumed. Engine:
  solidgas/redox.py; the browser carries the closed forms only, held against
  the Python bisection by tests/test_redox_port.py.

        material dependence of the steady state, and the only quantity in
        it: K > 1 means reduction outruns reoxidation.

The crossing

        
The Mars–van Krevelen pair. Reduction consumes lattice
        oxygen so its rate falls as the solid empties; oxidation consumes vacancies so
        its rate rises. Two opposed monotone curves meet once, and that is the whole
        model.

        
      


      

        
Where a carrier can be run

        
The crossing always exists on paper. Two things decide
        whether a real solid can sit at it, and the second axis here is the one
        the uniform assumption sets to 1 without saying so.

        
        

      

    


    

      

      


      

        
Cycling with memory

        
One inventory number cannot tell a vacancy that has just
        been made from one that already refused to come out. This carries two
        reservoirs instead: what an exposure can still reach, and what has stopped
        responding. Enter the measured per-cycle integrals and the two parameters
        follow — the first cycle fixes f, the later ones fix how much of each
        residual survived.

        

        

          
          
        

        

        

      


      

        
The experiment that decides it

        
Two samples at the same total VO, reached by
        different paths: one long reduction, and several short reduce/reoxidise
        cycles. A memoryless inventory says they must recover the same, because
        the total is its entire state. A locked reservoir says the cycled sample
        recovers less, by exactly the amount that has stopped responding — so
        the gap is the lock parameter, read straight off the experiment.

  Mater. 10 (2024); Iddir et al.; Wang et al. Parameters are stored in
  data/rutile_dft.json and data/redox.json.
  Engines: robin-yk/Solid-gas-thermosolver
  (solidgas/activeset.py, solidgas/statmech.py,
  solidgas/redox.py, solidgas/cycling.py); verified
  against the Python implementations, an 80-digit equilibrium reference and a 50-digit
  stat-mech reference by the repository test suite.
